To solve a problem at the airport: lost luggage.
Thursday, 6 May. Ajaccio airport, Corsica. Ioana and Julien have come for their honeymoon. The baggage carousel has stopped. Their suitcase hasn’t appeared. They go to the lost luggage desk.
Hello, sir. Our suitcase hasn’t arrived. There’s nothing left on the carousel.
I’m sorry. Do you have your baggage tag?
Yes, here it is. It’s a big red suitcase. Hasn’t anyone seen it?
(he looks at his computer) That’s strange… No red suitcase was checked in on this flight. Wait… Yes. It’s still in Lyon. It was held by customs.
By customs? But there’s nothing dangerous inside! There are only clothes and books.
According to the message, someone found something suspicious. A heavy glass object… Did anyone else pack your bags?
No, nobody. Well… my brother helped us close the suitcase. He insisted.
(he turns to Ioana) Radu? Radu touched our suitcase? Then I know what it is.
It will arrive tomorrow morning, on the first flight. In the meantime, do you have anything for the night?
No, nothing. I only have my handbag. I have no toothbrush, no pyjamas, no swimsuit.
No problem. Each passenger receives an essentials kit. Here’s a kit for each of you.
Thank you. And can you deliver the suitcase to our hotel? We don’t want to go anywhere tomorrow morning. It’s our honeymoon.
(he smiles) Congratulations! Fill in this form, and someone will bring it to you before noon. Several couples have had the same problem this week.
(on the way out, she takes her phone) I’m going to call my brother. He’s going to hear about this…

“Kel-kẽ”: nasal un at the end. “Quelque chose” = “kel-kuh-shohz”.
“Per-son”: the same word means “person” (une personne) and “nobody” (personne ne…). Context decides!
“Oh-kẽ” / “oh-kün”: the masculine is nasal, the feminine isn’t.
“Plü-zyuhr”: the s is read as z between vowels.
“Nee brosh nee pee-zha-ma”: each “ni” is said clearly, with stress.
Many indefinite pronouns have a negative “partner”. The negative always needs “ne” before the verb:
Il n’y a plus de pain.
French uses a double negative: “I don’t see anyone” = “Je NE vois PERSONNE”. English avoids double negatives (I see nobody), but French requires “ne” plus the second word — exactly like Romanian.
When “personne” or “rien” is the subject, it goes at the START, followed by “ne”:
In the passé composé: “Je n’ai RIEN vu” (rien before the past participle), but “Je n’ai vu PERSONNE” (personne after the participle).
With an adjective: quelque chose / rien / quelqu’un / personne + DE + adjective: “quelque chose de suspect”, “rien de dangereux”, “quelqu’un d’autre”.
Plusieurs couples ont eu ce problème.
Several couples have had this problem.
“Aucun” is almost always singular: “Je n’ai aucune idée” (I have no idea), not “aucunes idées”.
“Ne… que” is NOT a real negative: it means “only”. “Ni… ni” means “neither… nor”:
I have neither a toothbrush nor pyjamas.
After “ni… ni”, the indefinite article disappears: “Je n’ai ni frère ni sœur.” (I have neither a brother nor a sister.)

On the first evening, Ioana called her brother. Radu answered on the first ring, as if he had been waiting for the call. “So? Did you like my surprise?”
“Radu, our suitcase was held by customs for a whole night! I had nothing: no pyjamas, no toothbrush, no swimsuit!”

There was a silence. Then Radu said, in a very serious voice: “But the sarmale, did they arrive in good condition? Nobody ate them?” Ioana hung up. Julien was laughing so hard he had to sit down on the bed.
On Tuesday they hired a small car to visit the interior of the island. Julien wanted to see the mountain villages his grandfather Marcel had told him about; he had come to Corsica in his youth.

The road climbed and climbed, with bends everywhere. After an hour there were no more houses. After two hours there was nobody on the road any more. Only goats, which watched them pass without the slightest interest.
“Do you know where we are?” asked Ioana. Julien looked at his phone. No signal. The map showed nothing: no road, no village, just green. “I think we’re… nowhere,” he answered.

They drove on a little further. There was only a quarter of a tank left. Nobody knew where they were. Ioana was starting to worry, but she didn’t want to say anything, so as not to spoil the honeymoon.
At last, round a bend, they saw something: a little stone house, with smoke rising from the chimney. In front of the door, an old man was sitting on a chair, with a dog lying at his feet.
Julien stopped and wound down the window. “Hello, sir! Excuse me, we’re lost. Is there a village somewhere around here?”

The old man looked at them for a long time without saying anything. Then he got up, went into the house, and came back with three glasses and a bottle. “Nobody ever comes this way,” he said with a strong accent. “So when someone does, we have a drink.”
His name was Antoine. He was ninety, and he had lived alone in that house since his wife died. He had no television, no phone, no neighbours. Only his dog, his goats and his memories.
When Julien said he was from Lyon, and that his grandfather Marcel had come to these mountains in 1960, Antoine put down his glass. “Marcel? A tall blond fellow who played the accordion?”
Julien couldn’t believe his ears. His grandfather did play the accordion. He had taught it to him when he was little. That was even why Julien had become a musician.

“He spent a whole summer here,” Antoine said. “He was working on building the road. In the evenings he played for the whole village. Every girl in the village was in love with him. But he didn’t look at any of them: he talked all the time about a certain Rose, who was waiting for him in Marseille.”
Rose. Julien’s grandmother. He felt his eyes fill with tears. Ioana took his hand.

Antoine showed them the road to the village, five kilometres away. Before leaving, Julien took out his phone and played, on a little piano app, the only accordion song his grandfather had taught him. The old man closed his eyes and sang the words softly, in Corsican.

In the car, Ioana said: “Can you believe it? We were lost in the middle of nowhere, and we found someone who knew your grandfather.” Julien smiled. “With you, Ioana, I’m never really lost. There’s always someone waiting for us somewhere.”

On the last day, before their flight, they went back to see Antoine. This time they knew the way. They brought him fresh bread, cheese and a box of biscuits from Lyon. The old man said nothing, but he hugged Julien for a very long time.

On Sunday evening they came home to Lyon. On the stairs of the building, someone was waiting for them: Victor, sitting in front of their door like a guard. Madame Bernard came down with a hot soup. “Nobody has touched your piano,” she said. “But Victor slept on it every night. He was waiting for you.”

The next day, Julien called his mother in Annecy to tell her about Antoine. Brigitte was silent for a moment. Then she said: “Wait.” She came back with an old photo she had found among Marcel’s things after he died. Nobody had ever known who the people in the photo were.

She sent it by message. In the photo you could see a tall young blond man with an accordion, in the middle of a group of villagers. Next to him, a young man of about twenty-five was smiling, with a goat in his arms. On the back of the photo, a few words: “Corsica, summer 1960. With Antoine.”

Julien printed the photo that very day and posted it to the little mountain village, with a letter. He didn’t know if anyone would read it. But three weeks later, a postcard arrived at rue d’Austerlitz. There were only three words, written in a shaky hand: “Thank you. Come back soon.”

On her honeymoon, Ioana keeps a diary. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Friday. Our suitcase arrived at eleven o’clock. The delivery man told us that nobody at the airport had ever seen anything like it.
Inside, among our clothes, there was a big glass jar. A jar of sarmale. With a little note from Radu: “So that you don’t eat anything else on your honeymoon.”
Saturday. We went to a little mountain village. There was nobody in the streets, only cats and goats. Not a single tourist. Total silence.
In the only café in the village, there was just one old man. He spoke neither French nor English, only Corsican. But he offered us a glass of his wine, and we understood every word.
Sunday. Palombaggia beach. The water is so clear that you can see every fish. Julien said he had never seen a sea like it, not even in Marseille.
This evening we ate Radu’s sarmale on the hotel terrace, facing the sea. Several guests asked us what they were. We gave some to each of them.
I won’t tell anyone… but they were delicious. Nothing beats Granny’s sarmale. Not even in Corsica.
